newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: Israel still interested in Qatari gas - Enron.
newsitem.headline: Israel still interested in Qatari gas - Enron.

text.p: Israel is still interested in importing Qatari liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the U.S. Enron Corp, the managing director of the Enron Development Corporation said on Monday.

"The Israelis sent us another letter. They are still very interested in Qatari LNG," Carey Sloan told delegates at a gas conference in Abu Dhabi. "We have a heads of agreement on the table and we are continuing to proceed with that."

An Israeli National Infrastructure Ministry spokesman said in Tel Aviv on Thursday that Israel has informed Enron in a letter in September that it no longer has an exclusive agreement to negotiate with Qatar for LNG supplies for Israel.
Sloan did not elaborate on the second letter that he said Enron received from Israel.

Enron and Israel signed a memorandum of understanding in October 1995 granting the Houston-based company 180 days to finalise an agreement with Qatar for the supply of at least two million tonnes a year of natural gas.
The agreement gave Enron exclusivity in negotiations with Qatar during this 180-day period.

The Infrastructure Ministry spokesman said Israel decided not to renew the agreement with Enron since no deal was reached with Qatar during the 180-day period. However, he stressed, this did not mean that Enron could not continue to negotiate with Israel towards reaching a deal.
Sloan said Enron was planning to develop LNG from Qatar's oilfield for export to Aqaba in Jordan in the first quarter of the year 2001.

Qatar and Oman have forged ahead of other Gulf states in establishing economic ties with Israel but have stopped short of full diplomatic relations pending the resolution of all Arab-Israeli conflicts.

Qatar, meanwhile, has put further normalisation on hold, including postponing the opening of a trade office in Israel. This followed the recent outbreak of violence between Israelis and Palestinians that killed 75 people and cast doubts on the future of the Middle East peace process.
